lessons.unit: Unit 1: Analysing and displaying data
lessons.title: Mode, median and range
lessons.bigQuestion: What is the 'typical' number of brothers and sisters in our class, and how could we prove it?
objectives: Find the mode of numerical and non-numerical data
Find the median of an odd or even number of values
Find the range and say what it tells us
successCriteria: Find the mode and range of a list
Find the median, including when there are two middle values
Choose which average best describes a set of data and explain why
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: repeated measurements in experiments; Geography: rainfall data
lessons.smsc: Social: listening to everyone's data with respect; every pupil's answer counts

keywords.def: the value that appears most often
the middle value when the data is in order
largest value minus smallest value; it measures spread
a single value that represents a typical value in the data
a collection of facts or numbers

starter: Bismillah. Put these in order, smallest first: 12, 7, 19, 3, 7
Which number is exactly halfway between 14 and 20?
Write down a number that appears twice in this list: 4, 9, 2, 9, 5

teach.heading: Three ways to describe data
bullets: Median: the middle value, in order
Mode and median are averages; range is a spread
teach.note: Say bismillah and welcome the class. Ask: 'If I said the typical Year 7 has 2 siblings, what would I mean?' Take answers in the chat. Introduce the three words. Stress that range is NOT an average: it tells us how spread out the data is. Misconception: pupils give the range as '3 to 19' instead of 16.

teach.heading: Finding the median
bullets: Even count: halfway between the two middle values
teach.note: Model slowly. Cover the answer and ask pupils to predict each step.

model.problem: Find the median of 8, 3, 11, 5, 9, 4
steps: There are 6 values, an even number

teach.heading: Mode with words and numbers
bullets: Data can be words: favourite fruit
If every value appears once, there is no mode
teach.note: Show: apple, date, apple, banana, date, apple. Mode = apple. Then: 2, 4, 4, 7, 7 has two modes, 4 and 7. Ask: 'Can a set of words have a median?' (Not usually: words cannot be put in numerical order.)

teach.heading: Range is a spread, not a span
bullets: Bigger range means less consistent data
teach.note: Use two batters' scores to bring this alive: Ali 30, 32, 31 (range 2) and Bilal 5, 70, 18 (range 65). Who is more consistent? Ali.

teach.heading: Check: which is the median?
teach.note: Everyone answers on a mini-whiteboard or in the chat at the same time.

check.why: In order: 2, 4, 6, 7, 9, so the middle value is 6. A chose the middle of the unordered list; D is the mean.

practice: Find the mode, median and range of 5, 8, 2, 8, 6
Find the median of 12, 15, 11, 19, 14, 10
The ages of five cousins are 9, 11, 9, 14 and 12. Find the range and the mode.
independent: Core: Find the mode, median and range of 23, 18, 30, 18, 26, 21, 25
Extend: Five numbers have a median of 7, a mode of 4 and a range of 10. Find a possible set of numbers.
Stretch: Add one number to 3, 5, 8, 9 so that the median becomes 8. Is there more than one answer? Explain.
exit: Find the median of 4, 10, 7, 1
The range of a set of data is 12. The smallest value is 9. What is the largest value?
Which average can you use for 'favourite colour' data, and why?
lessons.homework: Record how many minutes you spend reading each day for a week, then find the mode, median and range.
lessons.send: Support: give data cards to physically order and a highlighter for the middle. Stretch: create data sets that meet given averages and range.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Analysing and displaying data
lessons.title: Pictograms, bar charts and bar-line charts
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do newspapers use charts instead of just printing the numbers?
objectives: Read and draw pictograms using a key
Draw bar charts and bar-line charts with labelled axes
Find the mode and range from a chart
successCriteria: Read values from a pictogram and a bar chart
Draw an accurate bar chart with a title, labels and equal gaps
Choose the best chart for a set of data and justify it
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: climate graphs; English: reading charts in non-fiction texts
lessons.smsc: Moral: charts should be honest and not mislead the reader

keywords.def: a chart that uses symbols to show frequency
explains what one symbol represents
how many times something happens
a chart of bars whose heights show frequency
a labelled line used to read values on a chart

starter: A symbol stands for 4 people. How many people do 3 symbols show?

teach.heading: Reading a pictogram
bullets: Half a symbol means half the value
Count whole symbols, then add parts
teach.note: Show a pictogram of books read: key 1 book symbol = 4 books. Monday 3½ symbols. Ask: 'How many books?' (14). Misconception: counting symbols as single items and ignoring the key.

model.problem: Key: one star = 6 pupils. Friday shows 2½ stars. How many pupils?

teach.heading: Drawing a bar chart
bullets: Title and labels on both axes
teach.note: Model on the shared whiteboard with this data: walk 9, car 6, bus 4, bike 2. Show why the scale must go up in equal steps. Ask: 'What scale would you choose if the biggest value was 45?'

model.problem: Draw a bar chart: walk 9, car 6, bus 4, bike 2
steps: Write a title: How pupils travel to school
Horizontal axis: type of travel; vertical: frequency
Draw bars of equal width with equal gaps
model.answer: Tallest bar = walk, so mode = walk

teach.heading: Bar-line charts
bullets: Useful for numerical data, e.g. goals scored
Read the height of each line
teach.note: Show goals per match: 0 goals 3 times, 1 goal 5 times, 2 goals 4 times, 3 goals 1 time. Ask for the mode (1 goal) and the range (3 − 0 = 3). Point out range uses the goals values, not the frequencies.

left.title: Bar chart
points: Categories such as transport or fruit

right.title: Bar-line chart
points: Numbers such as goals or siblings

teach.heading: Mode and range from a chart
bullets: Mode: the tallest bar or line
Range uses the data values, not the frequencies
teach.note: This is the most common error on this topic. Repeat it with a second example.

misconception.right: Range = biggest data value − smallest data value

teach.heading: Check: read the key
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: One circle = 8 cars. A row has 3 circles and a quarter of a circle. How many cars?
check.why: 3 × 8 = 24 and ¼ of 8 = 2, so 26. A forgets the key; D ignores the quarter.

practice: Key: one square = 10 votes. How many squares show 35 votes?
Draw a bar chart for favourite subject: maths 7, science 5, English 4, art 3
From a bar-line chart: 0 pets × 6, 1 pet × 9, 2 pets × 4, 3 pets × 2. Find the mode and range.
independent: Core: Draw a pictogram for books borrowed: Mon 12, Tue 8, Wed 14, Thu 6 using one symbol = 4 books
Extend: A pictogram uses one symbol = 5. Explain how you would show 23, and why this key makes it awkward. Suggest a better key.
Stretch: Design a misleading bar chart of the same data by changing the scale. Explain how it misleads.
exit: Key: one symbol = 6. How many symbols show 21?
Name two things every bar chart must have.
A bar chart's tallest bar is 'red' with frequency 12. What is the mode?
lessons.homework: Find a chart in a newspaper or website, sketch it and write two facts it shows and one question it leaves unanswered.
lessons.send: Support: pre-drawn axes with the scale marked. EAL: label bank for title/axis words. Stretch: compare two charts of the same data.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Analysing and displaying data
lessons.title: Tally charts and frequency tables
lessons.bigQuestion: What is the most efficient way to count a lot of data quickly and accurately?
objectives: Record data in a tally chart
Complete a frequency table
Find the mode and total frequency from a table
successCriteria: Use tally marks in fives correctly
Complete a frequency table and check the total
Spot and fix errors in someone else's tally chart
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: recording results; PE: recording scores
lessons.smsc: Social: careful, honest recording is a form of amanah (trust)

keywords.def: a mark used to count; every fifth mark crosses the four
a table showing each value and how often it occurs
the sum of all the frequencies
a group that data can be sorted into

starter: Key: one symbol = 4. How many does 2½ symbols show?
Name the two axes on a bar chart.

teach.heading: Tallying in fives
bullets: Four upright marks, the fifth crosses them
Gates of five are quick to count
Tick off each item as you go
teach.note: Model counting the shoe sizes of 20 people from a list, ticking each one off. Ask: 'Why cross the fifth mark?' (Fast counting in fives.)

steps: Size 3 appears 5 times: one gate of five

teach.heading: From tally to frequency
bullets: Total must equal the number of data items
teach.note: The total row is a self-check. If it doesn't match, something was missed.

teach.heading: Common slip
bullets: Count the gates, then the single marks
teach.note: Show a tally drawn with six upright lines and ask what went wrong.

misconception.right: A gate of five plus one: easier to count

teach.heading: Reading a frequency table
bullets: Mode: the value with the highest frequency
Do not confuse values and frequencies
teach.note: Ask: 'In a table of pets per family, what is the difference between the value 2 and the frequency 2?' Take two answers.

teach.heading: Check: total frequency
teach.note: Answer on whiteboards.

check.q: A table has frequencies 7, 12, 9 and 2. How many data items were collected?
check.why: 7 + 12 + 9 + 2 = 30. A counts the rows; B is the biggest frequency (that gives the mode).

practice: Make a tally chart for: red, blue, red, green, red, blue, yellow, red
Complete the frequency column and total for your tally
What is the mode colour?
independent: Core: Make a tally and frequency table for these dice scores: 1, 4, 6, 6, 2, 3, 6, 4, 5, 1, 6, 2, 4, 6, 3
Extend: A frequency table of 40 pupils has one frequency missing: 8, 11, ?, 9. Find it and explain your method.
Stretch: Two pupils tallied the same 25 results and got different totals. List three mistakes that could cause this and how to prevent each.
exit: Draw the tally for 12.
Frequencies are 4, 9, 6. What is the total frequency?
Which value is the mode: A (freq 4), B (freq 9) or C (freq 6)?
lessons.homework: Roll a dice (or use an online dice) 30 times and record the results in a tally and frequency table. Which score was the mode?
lessons.send: Support: data printed on cut-out cards to sort first. EAL: word bank tally/frequency/total. Stretch: design your own data-collection sheet.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Analysing and displaying data
lessons.title: Grouping data into class intervals
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we make sense of 30 different test scores without listing every one?
objectives: Group data into equal class intervals
Construct a grouped frequency table
Find the modal class
successCriteria: Put each value into the correct class
Build a grouped frequency table with equal classes that do not overlap
Explain what grouping gains and loses
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: grouping heights or masses of plants; Geography: population by age group
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at how patterns appear when we organise information

keywords.def: a group that data is sorted into, such as 10–19
data sorted into class intervals
the class interval with the highest frequency
data that can only take certain values, such as whole numbers

teach.heading: Why group data?
bullets: Too many different values to tally separately
teach.note: Show 20 test scores out of 50: 12, 25, 31, 44, 38, 27, 19, 33, 41, 36, 22, 29, 47, 35, 28, 16, 39, 30, 24, 33. Ask: 'Would a tally of every single score help?' (No: almost every score appears once.)

teach.heading: Choosing class intervals
teach.note: Ask: 'Which class does 20 go in if the classes were 10–20 and 20–30?' Show why overlapping classes cause problems.

teach.heading: Building the table
bullets: Tick off each value as you tally
teach.note: Work through the scores together. Pupils call out the class for each score.

teach.heading: The modal class
bullets: The class with the highest frequency
It is a class, not a single number
teach.note: Ask: 'Can we say the mode is 33 from the table alone?' No: once grouped, we only know the class.

teach.heading: Check: which class?
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Classes are 0–9, 10–19, 20–29. Which class does 20 belong in?
check.why: 20 lies from 20 to 29. A comes from thinking 'up to 20'; C is why classes must not overlap.

practice: Find the modal class
How many values are less than 20?
independent: Extend: Choose your own class intervals for 3, 18, 27, 41, 45, 52, 9, 33, 38, 47, 21, 56. Justify your choice.
Stretch: Explain why you cannot find the exact range from a grouped table, and find the largest possible range for the heights table.
exit: Which class does 30 go in: 20–29 or 30–39?
Frequencies are 3, 9, 5 for classes A, B, C. Which is the modal class?
Give one disadvantage of grouping data.
lessons.homework: Ask 15 family members or friends their age (or use a list of ages provided), group them into classes of width 10 and find the modal class.
lessons.send: Support: class labels pre-written in the table. Stretch: compare two different groupings of the same data.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Analysing and displaying data
lessons.title: Grouped bar charts for discrete and continuous data
lessons.bigQuestion: Should there be gaps between bars, and does it matter?
objectives: Distinguish discrete and continuous data
Draw a bar chart for grouped discrete data
Draw a frequency diagram for continuous data with no gaps
successCriteria: Say whether data is discrete or continuous
Draw a grouped bar chart with labelled class intervals
Explain why continuous data has no gaps between bars
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: measuring time, length and mass is continuous; PE: race times
lessons.smsc: Cultural: comparing data from different countries fairly

keywords.def: data that can only take particular values, often counted
data that can take any value in a range, usually measured
a bar chart for grouped continuous data with no gaps
a statement such as 10 ≤ t < 20 showing a range of values

starter: Which class does 19 go in: 10–19 or 20–29?
Is 'number of brothers' something you count or measure?

teach.heading: Counted or measured?
bullets: Shoe size is discrete; foot length is continuous
teach.note: Run a quick vote: number of pets, height, time to run 100 m, number of goals. Ask pupils to justify. Misconception: age is often treated as discrete, but age is continuous (we round it).

teach.heading: Writing continuous classes
bullets: 10 ≤ t < 20 means from 10 up to but not including 20
Every value fits in exactly one class
teach.note: Read the inequality aloud: 't is greater than or equal to 10 and less than 20'. Ask where 19.9 goes (10 ≤ t < 20) and where 20 goes (20 ≤ t < 30).

teach.heading: Drawing a frequency diagram
bullets: Continuous scale on the horizontal axis
Label the axis with the unit
teach.note: Model on the shared screen.

steps: Horizontal axis: time in seconds, scale 10 to 40
Bars from 20 to 30 (height 9) and 30 to 40 (height 6), touching

teach.heading: Gaps or no gaps?
teach.note: Ask: 'Why would a gap be wrong for time data?' Because a time of 19.99 s is still in the data: there is no value missing between bars.

misconception.wrong: Gaps between bars of a height chart
misconception.right: Bars touch, because heights can take any value

teach.heading: Check: discrete or continuous?
teach.note: Whiteboards up.

check.q: Which of these is continuous data?
options: Number of letters in a name
Number of cars in a car park
check.why: Mass is measured and can be any value. The others are counted or fixed sizes.

practice: Discrete or continuous: temperature, number of siblings, length of a leaf?
Write the class for 15 kg using classes 10 ≤ m < 20, 20 ≤ m < 30
Sketch the axes for a frequency diagram of times from 0 to 60 seconds.
independent: Core: Draw a frequency diagram: 0 ≤ h < 10: 3, 10 ≤ h < 20: 8, 20 ≤ h < 30: 5, 30 ≤ h < 40: 2 (h = hours of screen time per week)
Extend: Draw a grouped bar chart (with gaps) for goals per season: 0–4: 2 teams, 5–9: 6, 10–14: 9, 15–19: 3. Explain why this one has gaps.
Stretch: A pupil writes classes 1–2 m, 2–3 m, 3–4 m for jump distances. Explain the problem and rewrite them correctly.
exit: Is 'time to finish a race' discrete or continuous?
What does 20 ≤ t < 30 mean in words?
Should a chart of heights have gaps between the bars?
lessons.homework: Time how long 10 activities take you (to the nearest second), group the times into classes of 10 seconds and draw a frequency diagram.
lessons.send: Support: sorting cards for discrete/continuous before the chart. EAL: inequality phrases with examples. Stretch: classes of unequal width (and why they need care).

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Analysing and displaying data
lessons.title: The mean and comparing data sets
lessons.bigQuestion: Which of two cricketers is better, and how can averages help us decide fairly?
objectives: Calculate the mean of a set of data
Compare two sets of data using an average and the range
Decide which average is most appropriate
successCriteria: Calculate the mean accurately
Compare two data sets with one average and the range, in a sentence
Choose and justify the best average, including when there is an outlier
lessons.crossCurricular: PE: comparing performances; Science: mean of repeat readings
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness; judging people on evidence, not first impressions

keywords.def: total of the values divided by the number of values
a value much bigger or smaller than the rest
values are close together: a small range
say what is similar or different, using evidence

teach.heading: The mean
bullets: Divide by how many values there are
The mean shares the total out equally
teach.note: Use the 'levelling' idea: towers of cubes 2, 5, 8 levelled out to 5, 5, 5.

model.problem: Find the mean of 6, 9, 4, 11, 5

teach.heading: Outliers change the mean
bullets: One extreme value pulls the mean
Use the median when there is an outlier
teach.note: Salaries example: £20k, £22k, £25k, £21k, £200k. Mean £57.6k (misleading), median £22k. Ask: 'Which better describes a typical worker?'

teach.heading: Comparing two sets
bullets: Compare an average: who is higher overall?
Compare the range: who is more consistent?
teach.note: Model the sentence: 'Sara's mean score (7) is higher than Musa's (5), so Sara scored more on average. Musa's range (4) is smaller than Sara's (8), so Musa is more consistent.'

teach.heading: Writing a comparison
bullets: Good: give the average, the range and what they mean
teach.note: Show weak vs strong comparison. Ask pupils to improve a weak sentence in the chat.

misconception.wrong: Sara's range is bigger so she is better
misconception.right: A bigger range means less consistent, not better

teach.heading: Check: the mean
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.why: 3 + 8 + 10 + 7 = 28 and 28 ÷ 4 = 7. B forgets to divide; A is the median.

practice: Find the mean of 12, 15, 9, 14
Find the mean and median of 2, 3, 3, 4, 28. Which is more typical?
Two runners' times (s): A 14, 15, 16; B 12, 18, 15. Compare them.
independent: Core: Find the mean, median, mode and range of 8, 12, 5, 12, 9, 14
Extend: Compare these two classes' quiz scores using the mean and range: Class P 6, 8, 7, 9, 5; Class Q 3, 10, 9, 4, 9
Stretch: Four numbers have a mean of 6. Three of them are 4, 7 and 9. Find the fourth. Then change one number so the mean becomes 7.
exit: Find the mean of 10, 4, 7.
Which average would you use for house prices in a street with one mansion? Why?
What does a smaller range tell you?
lessons.homework: Find the mean, median and range of your last five scores in any quiz or game, then write two sentences comparing them with a friend's or family member's.
lessons.send: Support: calculator allowed for the totals, with a step frame. Stretch: reverse-mean problems.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Analysing and displaying data
lessons.title: Line graphs
lessons.bigQuestion: When does joining the points on a graph make sense, and when is it wrong?
objectives: Read values from a line graph
Draw a line graph for data over time
Describe trends using precise language
successCriteria: Read values and differences from a line graph
Plot a line graph accurately with time on the horizontal axis
Describe and explain a trend, and say when joining points is not valid
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: temperature and rainfall over a year; Science: cooling curves
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the changing seasons and the signs of Allah in creation

keywords.def: points joined by straight lines to show change over time
the general direction the data is moving
go up
go up and down without a clear pattern

starter: Read this scale: halfway between 20 and 30 is…
Which is continuous: time or number of pets?
Plot the point (3, 5): which axis first?

teach.heading: What a line graph shows
bullets: Time always on the horizontal axis
Joined points show the values in between
teach.note: Show a temperature graph for London from January to December. Ask: 'In which month was it warmest? When did it rise fastest?'

teach.heading: Reading the graph
bullets: Go up from the time, across to the value
teach.note: Model with average monthly temperatures in London: Jan 5 °C, Apr 11 °C, Jul 19 °C, Oct 12 °C.

model.problem: By how much did the temperature rise from January (5 °C) to July (19 °C)?

teach.heading: Describing trends
bullets: Then detail: the steepest part, peak, lowest point
teach.note: Model a sentence: 'The temperature increases from January to a peak of 19 °C in July, then decreases to 6 °C in December.'

teach.heading: When not to join points
bullets: Joining points suggests values in between
Categories (like favourite fruit) cannot be joined
teach.note: Ask: 'What would a line between apple and banana mean?' Nothing: so use a bar chart.

misconception.right: Bar chart for categories; line graph for change over time

teach.heading: Check: read the graph
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: A graph shows 120 visitors on Monday and 85 on Tuesday. What is the change?
check.why: 120 − 85 = 35 and it went down, so a decrease of 35. A has the wrong direction; C adds instead of subtracting.

practice: Plot a line graph of a plant's height: week 1 2 cm, week 2 3.5 cm, week 3 5 cm, week 4 7 cm
Read the height at week 3
Describe the trend in one sentence.
independent: Core: Draw a line graph of a city's temperature: 6 am 8 °C, 9 am 12 °C, 12 pm 17 °C, 3 pm 18 °C, 6 pm 14 °C, 9 pm 10 °C
Extend: Estimate the temperature at 10:30 am from your graph and explain why it is only an estimate.
Stretch: Draw a dual line graph comparing two cities' temperatures and write three comparison sentences with numbers.
exit: Which axis does time go on?
Write one sentence describing a graph that goes 10, 14, 19, 17.
Would you use a line graph for favourite sports? Why?
lessons.homework: Record the temperature (or use a weather site) at the same time each day for a week and draw a line graph with a trend sentence.
lessons.send: Support: pre-drawn axes and plotted points to join. EAL: trend vocabulary mat (rise, fall, peak, steady). Stretch: dual line graphs.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Analysing and displaying data
lessons.title: Dual and compound bar charts
lessons.bigQuestion: How can one chart compare two groups at the same time?
objectives: Read and draw dual bar charts
Read and draw compound (stacked) bar charts
Choose a chart to suit a purpose
successCriteria: Read values from dual and compound bar charts
Draw a dual bar chart with a key
Choose the best chart for a question and justify the choice
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: comparing two countries; Business: sales of two products
lessons.smsc: Social: comparing groups respectfully, without stereotyping

keywords.def: two bars side by side for each category to compare two groups
bars split into sections stacked on top of each other
shows which colour or shading belongs to which group
a part compared with the whole

starter: Gaps or no gaps for a chart of heights?

teach.heading: Dual bar charts
bullets: Two bars per category, side by side
A key shows which group is which
Best for comparing groups category by category
teach.note: Show boys and girls' favourite sport. Ask: 'Which sport had the biggest difference between groups?'

model.problem: Draw a dual bar chart: Year 7 / Year 8 reading hours: Mon 3/2, Tue 4/5, Wed 2/4
steps: Draw axes: day, and hours from 0 to 6
For Monday, draw Year 7 bar (3) and Year 8 bar (2) touching
Repeat for Tuesday and Wednesday, leaving gaps between days
Add a key and a title
model.answer: Year 8 read more on Tuesday and Wednesday

teach.heading: Compound bar charts
bullets: Read a section: top minus bottom
teach.note: Model reading a stacked bar: Tuesday bar has walk 0–6, bus 6–10, car 10–13. So bus = 10 − 6 = 4.

misconception.right: Bus = 10 − 6 = 4 (top minus bottom of the section)

teach.heading: Which chart for which question?
teach.note: Give three questions and ask which chart fits each.

head: Question
Best chart
rows: Did boys or girls prefer cricket more?
What fraction of each day's travel was by bus?
How did sales change over a year?

teach.heading: Check: read a compound bar
teach.note: Whiteboards up.

check.q: A stacked bar has sections ending at 5, 12 and 20. How big is the middle section?
check.why: 12 − 5 = 7. A reads the top of the section; C is the top section (20 − 12).

practice: From a dual bar chart: Class A 8 and Class B 11 chose football. What is the difference?
From a compound bar: sections end at 4, 9, 15. Find each section.
Which chart would you use to compare rainfall in Lahore and London each month?
independent: Core: Draw a dual bar chart for votes for school trip destinations: Zoo Y7 12 / Y8 9, Museum Y7 7 / Y8 10, Park Y7 6 / Y8 8
Extend: Draw a compound bar chart for the same data and say which question each chart answers more easily.
Stretch: Write a short report (three sentences with numbers) comparing Year 7 and Year 8 choices, and suggest which trip to book and why.
exit: What does a key do?
A section of a stacked bar goes from 6 to 14. What is its value?
Which chart compares two groups side by side?
lessons.homework: Ask two groups (e.g. adults and children at home or in your family) the same question and present the results in a dual bar chart.
lessons.send: Support: partly drawn charts to complete. Stretch: percentage compound bar charts where every bar is 100%.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Number skills
lessons.title: Mental maths and the priority of operations
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do two people sometimes get different answers to the same calculation?
objectives: Use the priority of operations, including brackets
Use mental strategies for multiplication and division
Use inverse operations to check answers
successCriteria: Calculate with two operations in the correct order
Calculate with brackets, powers and several operations
Insert brackets to make a calculation true
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: computers follow operator precedence; Science: using formulae
lessons.smsc: Moral: agreed rules let everyone reach the same truth

keywords.def: the agreed order: brackets, indices, ÷ and ×, then + and −
a reminder: Brackets, Indices, Division and Multiplication, Addition and Subtraction
the operation that undoes another, such as ÷ undoes ×
the result of multiplying

starter: Which chart would compare two groups side by side?

teach.heading: The order matters
teach.note: Poll: 2 + 3 × 4 = 20 or 14? Reveal 14 and explain that mathematicians agreed this rule so everyone gets the same answer. Calculators follow it too.

teach.heading: BIDMAS
bullets: Division and Multiplication: left to right
Addition and Subtraction: left to right

hook.text: A news headline says '2 million people visited'. The exact number was 1,548,207. Is the headline honest? What should it say?

Write six million and forty in figures.

Look at the next digit: 5 or more rounds up

teach.heading: Large numbers
bullets: Nearest 1000: look at the hundreds digit
Nearest million: look at the hundred thousands digit

teach.heading: Estimating
bullets: Round each number to 1 significant figure
teach.note: Estimates catch keying errors on a calculator.

model.problem: Estimate 4,872 + 3,119.

teach.heading: Check: rounding
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.why: The hundredths digit is 4, so round down to 27.6. 27.7 comes from rounding twice (49 then 5); 28.0 is to the nearest whole; 27.65 is 2 d.p.

practice.model: 48,350 lies between 48,000 and 49,000. The hundreds digit is 3, less than 5, so round down: 48,000.

independent.q: Core: Round 3,456,789 to the nearest (a) 10 (b) 1000 (c) 100,000 (d) million.
independent.model: (a) Ones digit 9 rounds the tens up: 3,456,790. (b) Hundreds digit 7 rounds up: 3,457,000. (c) Ten thousands digit 5 rounds up: 3,500,000. (d) Hundred thousands digit 4 rounds down: 3,000,000.

exit.q: Round 5.083 to 1 decimal place.

keywords.def: a list of numbers or shapes in order that follow a rule
one number in a sequence
how to get from one term to the next
goes up or down by the same amount each time
going up

hook.text: Matchstick squares in a row: 1 square uses 4 sticks, 2 squares use 7, 3 squares use 10. How many sticks for 10 squares?
hook.a: The rule is +3, so 4, 7, 10, 13, ... The 10th term is 31. Later we find a quicker way than counting on.

teach.heading: Term-to-term rules
bullets: Look at the difference between terms
teach.note: Write the differences under each gap. Ask: is the difference always the same?

model.problem: Find the missing terms: __, 13, 20, __, 34

teach.heading: Linear or not?
bullets: Non-linear: for example ×2, or square numbers
teach.note: Sort as a class. 1, 4, 9, 16 has differences 3, 5, 7: not linear.

teach.heading: Is it in the sequence?
bullets: Count on with the rule, or look for a pattern
4, 7, 10, 13: all are one more than a multiple of 3
teach.note: Ask: is 50 in 4, 7, 10, ...? 49 is not a multiple of 3, so no.

misconception.right: It has term-to-term rule '+2'. The letter n comes later for position-to-term rules.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: What is the next term in 81, 27, 9, 3, ...?
check.why: The rule is ÷3, so 3 ÷ 3 = 1. Choosing 0 or −3 means a subtracting pattern was assumed.

practice.model: Differences: 19 − 12 = 7, 26 − 19 = 7, 33 − 26 = 7, so the rule is +7. Next terms: 33 + 7 = 40, 40 + 7 = 47.

practice.a: No: the rule is ×3, the differences are 2, 6, 18.

independent.q: Core: First term 6, rule +5. Write the first five terms.

independent.q: Extend: In the matchstick pattern 4, 7, 10, ..., how many squares can you make with 40 sticks?

exit.q: Big question: how could you find the 20th term of 4, 7, 10, 13 without writing them all?
exit.a: Start at 4 and add 3 nineteen times: 4 + 19 × 3 = 61.

practice.model: Input 6. Step 1: 6 × 5 = 30. Step 2: 30 − 4 = 26. Output 26.

exit.q: Write 'multiply n by 5 then subtract 2'.

keywords.def: both sides have the same value
a statement that is true only for some values of the letter
a statement true for every value; uses ≡
always equal in value
find the value that makes an equation true

hook.text: True or false: 3 + 4 = 7 + 2? Many pupils say 'true'. Why might they?
hook.a: False: the left is 7 and the right is 9. Some read = as 'the answer is' instead of 'the same as'.

teach.note: Picture a balance scale: each side must weigh the same. Fill the gap: 9 + 6 = __ + 8 (7).

misconception.right: The left side is 15, so __ + 8 must be 15: the gap is 7

bullets: x + 7 = 12 is true only when x = 5
teach.note: Do the same to both sides to keep the balance.

model.problem: Solve 4m = 36.

teach.heading: Identities and ≡
teach.note: Test with x = 1, 5, 10: both sides always match.

teach.heading: Equation or identity?
teach.note: Teams poll: equation or identity for each card, then reveal.

teach.heading: Check
bullets: Is it true for every value?
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.why: y + y + y + y + y is always 5y. The others are true only for one value of the letter.

practice.model: Left: 6 × 4 = 24. Right: 30 − 6 = 24. Both sides are 24, so the statement is true.

independent.model: (a) Subtract 12 from both sides: a = 18. (b) Divide both sides by 7: b = 9. (c) Add 4.5: c = 6.5. (d) Multiply by 3: d = 33.

successCriteria: All: measure acute and obtuse angles to the nearest degree
Most: draw an angle of a given size
Some: measure or draw a reflex angle using 360° minus the angle inside
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: measuring bearings on maps uses the same skill
lessons.smsc: Moral: itqan (إِتْقَان), doing even a small task carefully and accurately

keywords.def: a tool for measuring and drawing angles
the zero line of the protractor, placed along one arm
the numbers round the edge; a protractor has two
more than 180° but less than 360°

hook.text: A protractor only shows 0° to 180°. How could you use it to draw an angle of 250°?
hook.a: Draw 360 - 250 = 110° and mark the reflex angle on the outside.

teach.heading: Measuring
teach.note: Show on the visualiser with a real protractor.

model.problem: Measure angle ABC.
steps: Put the centre cross exactly on the vertex B
Line up the zero line with arm BA
Count up from 0° on the scale that starts at BA
Read where arm BC crosses; check: acute or obtuse?
model.answer: Use the scale that starts at 0 on your arm

teach.heading: Two scales
bullets: The scales always add up to 180°
teach.note: Ask: if one scale says 50, what does the other say? 130.

misconception.wrong: The angle looks acute but I read 130° from the outer scale
misconception.right: Start at 0° on the arm you lined up: an acute angle reads less than 90°, here 50°

teach.heading: Drawing an angle
teach.note: Pupils draw along with you.

model.problem: Draw angle PQR = 65°.
steps: Draw arm QR with a ruler, at least 7 cm
Centre on Q, zero line on QR
Mark a dot at 65° on the scale starting at R
Join Q to the dot and label 65°
model.answer: Check: it looks less than a right angle

teach.heading: Reflex angles
teach.note: A protractor cannot draw a reflex angle directly.

model.problem: Draw a reflex angle of 230°.
steps: Mark the outside angle with an arc and label it 230°

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: The inside angle is 48°. What is the reflex angle at the same vertex?
check.why: 360 - 48 = 312. 132° is 180 - 48: that is the angle on a straight line, not round a point.

practice.q: An angle measures 72°. A pupil writes 108°. What went wrong?
practice.model:
72 + 108 = 180: the two scales always add up to 180°.
The angle is acute, so 72° is correct; 108° came from the other scale.

practice.q: Draw an angle of 140°. Which type is it?
To draw 300°, what angle do you draw first?

independent.q: Core: Measure the six angles a to f on the printable angle sheet, then draw angles of 40°, 125° and 250°.
independent.a: Sheet: a 35°, b 118°, c 90°, d 162°, e 205°, f 330° (accept ± 2°). 250° is drawn as 110° inside with the outside marked.
independent.model:
Angle a: centre on the vertex, zero line on the lower arm, read the inner scale from 0: 35°.
It looks acute, so 35° (not 145°) is sensible.

independent.q: Extend: Without measuring, explain why angles of 175° and 185° look almost the same.
independent.a: Both are 5° from a straight line (180°), one on each side.

independent.q: Stretch: Draw triangle ABC with AB = 8 cm, angle A = 50° and angle B = 60°. Measure angle C. What should it be?
independent.a: 70°, because the angles in a triangle add up to 180°

exit.q: The inside angle is 100°. The reflex angle is:
Where does the centre cross of the protractor go?
exit.a: On the vertex of the angle

exit.q: Big question: why do the two scales cause wrong answers, and how do you avoid it?
exit.a: Each angle can be read as x or 180 - x; start from 0 on your arm and decide acute or obtuse first.

the steps that show your method
a point earned for a correct step or answer
the opposite operation, used to check

lessons.title: Constructing triangles: two sides and the included angle (SAS)
lessons.bigQuestion: If I tell you two sides and one angle, is there only one triangle you can draw?
objectives: To understand how to construct a triangle accurately from two sides and the angle between them
successCriteria: All: draw a line of a given length to the nearest millimetre
Most: construct a triangle from two sides and the included angle (SAS)
Some: explain why two sides and an angle that is not between them may give two triangles
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and technology: accurate drawings are made before anything is built
lessons.smsc: Moral: itqan (إِتْقَان), doing work carefully and well

keywords.def: draw accurately with a ruler, protractor or compasses
the angle between two given sides
a quick labelled drawing, not to scale
lengths within 1 mm and angles within 1°

hook.text: Two sides of a triangle are 6 cm and 4 cm. How many different triangles could you draw? What one extra fact would fix it?
hook.a: Infinitely many; the angle between the two sides fixes it.

starter.q: The inside angle is 35°. The reflex angle?

teach.heading: Sketch first
bullets: Decide which side to draw first
teach.note: A sketch avoids putting the angle at the wrong vertex.

teach.heading: SAS model
teach.note: Pupils follow on paper as you draw.

model.problem: Construct triangle ABC with AB = 7 cm, angle A = 40° and AC = 5 cm.
steps: Draw AB = 7 cm with a ruler
At A, measure 40° and draw a long faint line
Measure 5 cm along it from A and mark C

teach.heading: Where is the angle?
teach.note: The included angle is at the vertex the two sides share.

misconception.wrong: Measure the angle at B when it is given at A
misconception.right: The included angle is between the two given sides, at the vertex they share

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: Triangle PQR has PQ = 6 cm and QR = 8 cm. Which angle is the included angle?
check.why: Q is the vertex shared by PQ and QR, so angle Q is between them. P and R are at the far ends.

teach.heading: How accurate?
teach.note: Exam markers check with a ruler and protractor.

practice.q: Construct triangle XYZ with XY = 6 cm, angle X = 70° and XZ = 6 cm. Measure YZ and angles Y and Z.
practice.a: YZ ≈ 6.9 cm; angles Y and Z are both 55°
practice.model:
Draw XY = 6 cm, measure 70° at X, mark 6 cm along the arm, join to Y.
XY = XZ, so the triangle is isosceles: (180 - 70) ÷ 2 = 55° each.

practice.q: Construct triangle DEF with DE = 5 cm, angle E = 90° and EF = 12 cm. Measure DF.

independent.q: Core: Construct each triangle and measure the third side: (a) AB = 8 cm, angle A = 60°, AC = 8 cm (b) PQ = 9 cm, angle P = 35°, PR = 6 cm (c) KL = 7.5 cm, angle K = 110°, KM = 4 cm
independent.a: (a) 8 cm (b) QR ≈ 5.3 cm (c) LM ≈ 9.6 cm (accept ± 2 mm)
independent.model:
(a) Two 8 cm sides with 60° between them: the other angles are (180 - 60) ÷ 2 = 60° too.
The triangle is equilateral, so the third side is also 8 cm.

independent.q: Extend: Construct a rhombus with sides of 5 cm and one angle of 50°. Measure the shorter diagonal.
Stretch: AB = 7 cm, angle A = 40° and BC = 5 cm. Construct both possible triangles. Why are there two?
independent.a: An arc of 5 cm from B cuts the 40° line at A in two places, so C has two positions: the angle is not between the given sides.

exit.q: Which set of facts fixes exactly one triangle?
exit.a: B) two sides and the angle between them
options: two sides and the angle between them

exit.q: How accurate must a constructed length be?
Big question: if I give you two sides and one angle, is there only one triangle?
exit.a: Yes, if the angle is between the two sides (SAS); otherwise there may be two.

lessons.send: Support: pre-drawn first side and a step card. EAL: 'construct', 'included', 'sketch'. Stretch: the ambiguous case in the stretch task.

lessons.title: Constructing triangles: two angles and the included side (ASA)
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do two angles and one side fix a triangle, but three angles do not?
objectives: To understand how to construct a triangle accurately from two angles and the side between them
successCriteria: All: construct a triangle from two angles and the included side (ASA)
Most: calculate the third angle and check it by measuring
Some: explain why three angles alone give triangles of any size

keywords.def: the side between the two given angles
the angles in a triangle add up to 180°
the same shape but a different size
one of the two lines that make an angle

hook.text: Can two triangles have exactly the same three angles but be different sizes?
hook.a: Yes: they are similar; angles alone do not fix the size.

starter.q: The included angle between AB and BC

teach.heading: ASA model
teach.note: Both angles open towards the same side of the line.

model.problem: Construct triangle ABC with AB = 6 cm, angle A = 50° and angle B = 70°.
steps: At A, draw a long faint line at 50°
At B, draw a long faint line at 70° on the same side
The lines cross at C: label it

teach.heading: Three angles are not enough
teach.note: Draw both on screen.

teach.heading: Same side
bullets: Both arms point the same way
teach.note: Otherwise the lines go apart.

misconception.wrong: Draw angle B below the line and angle A above it
misconception.right: Both angles open towards the same side of AB, or the arms never meet

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: Angles of 100° and 90° are given at the two ends of a side. What happens?
options: the arms never meet: no triangle
check.why: 100 + 90 = 190, more than 180°, so the arms move apart. Two angles must add up to less than 180°.

practice.q: Construct triangle PQR with PQ = 7 cm, angle P = 45° and angle Q = 45°. Find angle R and measure PR.
practice.model:
180 - 45 - 45 = 90, so R is a right angle.
The base angles are equal, so PR = QR: measure about 4.9 cm.

practice.q: Angles of 35° and 120° are at the ends of a 5 cm side. Find the third angle.

independent.q: Core: Calculate the third angle, then construct and measure the other two sides: (a) AB = 8 cm, angle A = 30°, angle B = 60° (b) XY = 5.5 cm, angle X = 75°, angle Y = 75° (c) DE = 6 cm, angle D = 110°, angle E = 40°
independent.a: (a) C = 90°; AC ≈ 6.9 cm, BC = 4.0 cm (b) Z = 30°; XZ = YZ ≈ 10.6 cm (c) F = 30°; DF ≈ 7.7 cm, EF ≈ 11.3 cm (accept ± 2 mm)
independent.model:
(a) 180 - 30 - 60 = 90, so angle C = 90°.
Draw AB = 8 cm, 30° at A and 60° at B on the same side; they meet at C.
BC measures 4 cm: half of AB, as in every 30°, 60°, 90° triangle.

independent.q: Extend: Explain why angles of 95° and 85° cannot be the two angles at the ends of a side.
independent.a: 95 + 85 = 180, so the arms are parallel and never meet.

independent.q: Stretch: AB = 6 cm, angle A = 40° and angle C = 80°, where C is not on AB. How can you still construct it?
independent.a: Angle B = 180 - 40 - 80 = 60°; then use ASA with AB, angle A = 40° and angle B = 60°.

exit.q: Two angles at the ends of a side are 60° and 50°. The third angle is:
Name the side between angles P and Q.
Big question: why do two angles and a side fix a triangle, but three angles do not?
exit.a: Two angles and the side between them fix where the third vertex is; three angles fix only the shape, so the size can change.

lessons.homework: Construct three ASA triangles from the portal sheet; calculate and then measure the third angle of each.

lessons.bigQuestion: How can compasses find a point that is exactly 5 cm from one place and 4 cm from another?

keywords.def: a tool for drawing circles and arcs
part of a circle
the distance from the centre of a circle to its edge
the two shorter sides must add up to more than the longest side

hook.text: Can you make a triangle from sticks of 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm? What about 3 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm?
hook.a: No to both: 3 + 4 < 8, and 3 + 5 = 8 lies flat.

starter.q: The angle sum of a triangle
Third angle when two are 52° and 77°

teach.heading: SSS model
teach.note: Pupils draw along with you.

model.problem: Construct triangle ABC with AB = 6 cm, BC = 5 cm and AC = 4 cm.
steps: Set compasses to 4 cm: arc from A
Set compasses to 5 cm: arc from B
Join A and B to the crossing point C

teach.heading: Why the arcs work
bullets: Every point on the 4 cm arc is 4 cm from A
Every point on the 5 cm arc is 5 cm from B
teach.note: This answers the big question.

teach.heading: Can it be a triangle?
bullets: Two shorter sides must beat the longest
teach.note: Pupils sort, then we check.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.why: 5 + 6 = 11, more than 10. In the others the two shorter sides add up to less than, or exactly, the longest side.

teach.heading: Keep the arcs
teach.note: In an exam, rubbed-out arcs lose the construction marks.

misconception.wrong: Rub out the arcs to make it neat
misconception.right: Leave the arcs: they show it was constructed, not guessed

practice.q: Construct an equilateral triangle with sides of 7 cm.
practice.model:
Draw 7 cm. Keep the compasses at 7 cm and draw an arc from each end.
Join both ends to the crossing point: all sides 7 cm, so all angles 60°.

practice.q: Construct triangle PQR with PQ = 8 cm, QR = 6 cm and PR = 10 cm. Measure the largest angle.
Can 2.5 cm, 3.5 cm and 6 cm make a triangle?
practice.a: No: 2.5 + 3.5 = 6, so it would lie flat.

independent.q: Core: Construct each triangle with ruler and compasses, leaving the arcs, and measure the largest angle: (a) 5 cm, 5 cm, 5 cm (b) 7 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm (c) 9 cm, 6 cm, 6 cm
independent.model:
(b) Draw the longest side, 7 cm, first.
Arc of 4 cm from one end, arc of 5 cm from the other; join both ends to the crossing.
The largest angle is opposite the 7 cm side.

independent.q: Extend: Construct a kite with sides 5 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm and 8 cm whose short diagonal is 6 cm.
independent.a: Draw the 6 cm diagonal; arcs of 5 cm from both ends on one side and 8 cm from both ends on the other; join.

independent.q: Stretch: A triangle has sides of 4 cm, 9 cm and x cm, where x is a whole number. List every possible value of x.
independent.a: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 (x must be more than 5 and less than 13)

exit.q: Can 3 cm, 4 cm and 9 cm make a triangle?
To draw a side of 6 cm with an arc, set the compasses to:
Big question: how can compasses find a point 5 cm from one place and 4 cm from another?
exit.a: Draw an arc of radius 5 cm from the first and 4 cm from the second: where they cross is the point.

lessons.title: Constructing the perpendicular bisector of a line segment
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you find the exact middle of a line without measuring?
objectives: To understand how to construct a perpendicular bisector with compasses and why it works
successCriteria: All: construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment, leaving the arcs
Most: check that it meets the segment at the midpoint at 90°
Some: explain why every point on it is the same distance from both ends
lessons.smsc: Moral: 'adl (عَدْل), fairness: the perpendicular bisector marks the places that are fair to both sides

keywords.def: cut into two equal parts
the line that cuts a segment in half at right angles
the point exactly halfway along a line segment
the same distance from two or more places

hook.text: Two wells are 8 km apart. Where could you stand to be exactly the same distance from both? Is there more than one place?
hook.a: Anywhere on the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them: a whole line of places.

starter.q: Can 4 cm, 5 cm and 10 cm make a triangle?
The angle sum of a triangle

teach.heading: The construction
bullets: Compasses more than half the line
teach.note: Model live; pupils follow.

model.problem: Construct the perpendicular bisector of AB = 8 cm.
steps: Open the compasses to more than half of AB, for example 5 cm
Draw arcs above and below the line from A
Keep the radius: arcs above and below from B
Join the two crossing points with a ruler
model.answer: It crosses AB at the midpoint, 4 cm from each end, at 90°

teach.heading: Why it works
bullets: Each crossing point is 5 cm from A and from B
The four arcs make a rhombus
A rhombus's diagonals cross at right angles and bisect each other
teach.note: The perpendicular bisector is every point equidistant from A and B.

teach.heading: Same radius
teach.note: A changed radius gives a line that misses the midpoint.

misconception.wrong: Change the compass width between A and B
misconception.right: Use the same radius from both ends, or the line misses the midpoint

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: Compasses are set to 3 cm for a 10 cm line. What happens?
check.why: 3 + 3 = 6, less than 10, so the arcs cannot reach each other. Use more than half the line: more than 5 cm.

practice.q: Construct the perpendicular bisector of a 6 cm line. Measure each half and the angle.
practice.model:
Compasses at about 4 cm; arcs from both ends above and below; join the crossings.
Measure 3 cm and 3 cm and check 90° with a protractor.

practice.q: Point P is on the perpendicular bisector of CD and PC = 7 cm. Find PD.

independent.q: Core: (a) Draw AB = 10 cm and construct its perpendicular bisector. (b) Mark the midpoint M and measure AM. (c) Mark any point P on the bisector; measure PA and PB. (d) Draw any triangle and construct the perpendicular bisectors of two of its sides.
independent.a: (a) arcs visible (b) AM = 5 cm (c) PA = PB (d) the bisectors cross at a point the same distance from all three vertices
independent.model: (a) Compasses at 6 cm. Arcs from A and from B, above and below; join the two crossings with a ruler.

independent.q: Extend: Two villages A and B are 6 km apart (1 cm = 1 km). A well must be the same distance from both and 5 km from A. Construct its possible positions.
independent.a: Construct the perpendicular bisector of AB; an arc of 5 cm from A cuts it in two places, each 4 km from the midpoint.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why the three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle meet at one point.
independent.a: Where two meet, the point is equidistant from all three vertices, so it must also lie on the third bisector.

exit.q: The perpendicular bisector of AB crosses AB at:
Q is on the perpendicular bisector of EF and QE = 4.5 cm. Find QF.
Big question: how can you find the exact middle of a line without measuring?
exit.a: Construct the perpendicular bisector with equal arcs from both ends: it crosses at the midpoint.

lessons.bigQuestion: How can you split any angle exactly in half without a protractor?
objectives: To understand how to bisect an angle with compasses and why the construction works

keywords.def: a line that cuts an angle into two equal angles
part of a circle
draw accurately with compasses and a ruler
with all sides equal and all angles 60°

hook.text: You have compasses and a ruler but no protractor. How could you draw an angle of exactly 30°?
hook.a: Construct an equilateral triangle for 60°, then bisect that angle.

starter.q: P is on the perpendicular bisector of AB and PA = 6 cm. PB?

teach.heading: Bisecting an angle
bullets: Then equal arcs from the arms
teach.note: Model with a 70° angle.

model.problem: Bisect angle ABC = 70°.
steps: Arc from B cutting both arms at P and Q
Same radius: arcs from P and from Q crossing inside the angle
Join B to the crossing point
model.answer: Two angles of 35°: check with a protractor

teach.heading: Why it works
bullets: BP = BQ, and the two small arcs are equal
So two congruent triangles share the bisector
Their angles at B are equal
teach.note: Congruent: identical in shape and size.

teach.heading: Special angles
teach.note: Pupils copy the table.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: Bisecting a reflex angle of 240° gives:
check.why: Half of 240 is 120. 60° would come from bisecting the 120° angle on the other side.

practice.q: Draw an angle of 80° and bisect it with compasses.
practice.model:
Arc from the vertex across both arms.
Equal arcs from the two crossing points; join the vertex to where they meet.
Check: 40° each.

practice.q: Construct an angle of 60° with compasses and a ruler.
practice.a: Arc from the vertex; same radius from where it cuts the line; join the vertex to the crossing.

independent.q: Core: (a) Draw angles of 50°, 130° and 90° and bisect each. (b) Construct an angle of 30° without a protractor. (c) Measure your halves and record any error.
independent.a: (a) 25°, 65°, 45° (b) construct 60°, then bisect (c) within 1° is accurate
independent.model: (a) For 130°: arc from the vertex across both arms; equal arcs from those points; join the vertex to the crossing; measure 65° each.

independent.q: Extend: Construct an angle of 15° with compasses and a ruler only.
independent.a: Construct 60°, bisect to 30°, bisect again to 15°.

independent.q: Stretch: Construct triangle ABC with AB = 7 cm, BC = 6 cm and AC = 5 cm. Bisect all three angles. What do you notice?
independent.a: The three bisectors meet at one point: the centre of the circle that touches all three sides.

exit.q: Bisecting a 90° angle gives:
Which angle do you bisect to get 30°?
Big question: how can you halve any angle without a protractor?
exit.a: Equal arcs from the vertex, then from the arms; the line to the crossing splits it exactly in half.
